Patient Vignette: Mrs. G.

Mrs. G. is a 79-year-old widow who lives alone in the small apartment above the tailor shop she has run for fifty years. She presents for her first session wearing a perfectly pressed cardigan, her white hair pinned back with the precision of someone who has spent a lifetime measuring twice and cutting once. She sits very still, hands folded in her lap, and begins her story not with the war, but with the cloth.

She was twenty-four when she was conscripted as a military seamstress for the army. It was not a choice. She remembers the cold, damp barracks where she and the other women worked sixteen-hour shifts, repairing uniforms and sewing insignia onto tunics for soldiers who would be sent to the front. She speaks of the fabric—rough wool, stiff canvas, the smell of sweat and mud that clung to every garment. She remembers the blood. Not gore, not violence she witnessed directly, but the stains. The brown, rust-colored patches on the trousers and jackets that came back for mending. She would have to cut around them, discarding the ruined pieces, stitching new cloth into the holes. She never knew whose blood it was. She never knew if the soldier lived or died. But she learned to see that color everywhere.

After the war, she married a quiet man, a carpenter. She never told him about the barracks. She opened her shop, measured clients for suits and wedding dresses, and for decades, she managed. She raised two children. She buried her husband fifteen years ago. The shop became her life.

But now, at seventy-nine, the past is no longer staying buried. It began three years ago, when a young veteran came in for a uniform alteration. He was in the reserves, needing his dress blues let out. Mrs. G. took his measurements, her fingers brushing the heavy wool of the jacket. The smell hit her first—that particular blend of dry-cleaning chemicals and old fabric. Then she saw the sleeve. A small, dark spot near the cuff. Not blood, just a drop of coffee, but her hands began to shake. She excused herself to the back room, locked the door, and stood in the dark for ten minutes, breathing in the scent of thread and dust, trying to remember where she was.

Now it happens all the time. A customer’s coat with a frayed cuff sends her back to the barracks. The sound of a sewing machine—her own machine—triggers a surge of adrenaline so sharp she has to stop working. She has become afraid of her own hands. She will be threading a needle and suddenly see the brown stains, feel the weight of a dead man's uniform in her lap. She has nightmares of the barracks, but in the dreams, she is not a young woman. She is seventy-nine, still sewing, and the soldiers are ghosts who stand silently, waiting for their mended clothes.

She has stopped taking new orders. She tells her children she is tired. She has lost twelve pounds in four months because she cannot bear to sit at her sewing table to eat. The shop is dusty. Unfinished alterations hang on the rack like forgotten men. She spends her days in the armchair by the window, watching the street, her hands gripping the armrests so tightly her knuckles are white. She is not crying. She is not angry. She is simply waiting, though she does not know for what. She came to therapy because her daughter found her on the floor of the shop, sobbing, holding a pair of old military trousers she had found in a box of donations. Mrs. G. could not explain why she was crying. She only knew that the brown stains were back, and this time, they would not wash out.
